description: I'm a tech builder who is keen to see how to make meaningful products that can impact the world positively.
summary:
Every dry season, farmers across Southeast Asia clear fields with fire, causing cross-border haze, peat fires and soil loss. For those of us who live in Southeast Asia, the haze massively impacts our health and disrupts our daily routines during this time.

Field of View is a crop-planning tool for farmers in Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia, built on NASA satellite data. A farmer and an agriculture officer use it together on one phone, in English, Thai, Bahasa Indonesia or Bahasa Melayu.

The farmer picks a district, answers a few plain questions and chooses up to three goals. The tool then shows their farm's year as seen from space (rain from NASA GPM, fire on farmland nearby from NASA FIRMS and, where its quality allows, topsoil moisture from SMAP), one practical no-burn change to try next season compared with what they do now, what could go wrong, and what to ask their agriculture officer.

It answers the challenge by turning long-term NASA Earth observations into crop and crop-waste choices that protect soil and avoid burning. It is built around farmers' own priorities and leaves the final call to farmers and local experts.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Landing page: an interactive map of six farming areas over NASA GIBS satellite imagery from each area's worst burning day, with every NASA FIRMS fire detection from 2015 to 2025.

Farmer tool, in four short steps:

A first-time visitor sees a finished sample plan, then makes their own.

1. Place: choose a district. A small map over a Sentinel-2 satellite image shows where satellites saw fire on farmland and scrub nearby (forest fire is left out).

2. Farm: three or four plain questions about crop waste, slope, standing water, irrigation and cattle. Burning is illegal or restricted in all three countries, so the tool asks what happens to crop waste, with no answer preselected, and never puts that answer in a shared link.

3. Goals: pick up to three, such as no smoke, less fertiliser to buy, protect the soil or peat, safe to try, money soon, or animal feed.

4. Plan: the farm's year now (rain, farm fire seen from space, what is in the field each month), then one change to try, shown as a short picture guide of the field month by month (harvest without fire, sow beans, leave the straw, grow rice as usual) and compared with current practice as Better, Same or Worse for each goal, with when to start, what you need, the work involved, what could go wrong, and what to ask the agriculture officer. Each option also says how proven it is in that area (farmers here already do it, a local programme supports it, it has been tried nearby, or we found no record yet) with links to the sources. Multi-year programmes and anything the farmer already does are never the headline suggestion. The plan can be shared as a link or printed as one page with a box for the officer's notes.

SIX AREAS, CHOSEN WITH SATELLITE DATA

We screened 77 Thai provinces and 519 Indonesian districts (491 had fire detections) by NASA FIRMS fire on non-forest land, after removing forest and plantation fire with ESA WorldCover land cover. Our first Thai pick, Nan, failed this test (70-90% of its fire was on tree cover), so we replaced it.

- Nakhon Sawan, Thailand: irrigated rice on the central plains (#1 of 77 provinces for fire on cropland, 2023-24). The tool notes that satellites cannot tell rice-straw fire from sugarcane fire, and is limited to rice-plain districts.

- MADA rice area, Kedah, Malaysia: Malaysia's largest rice-growing area, double-cropped, with straw burned between seasons.

- Pulang Pisau, Central Kalimantan: rice and food crops on peat (#1 of 519 districts for non-forest fire, mostly burnt scrub on peat).

- Ogan Komering Ilir, South Sumatra: swamp rice (#2 for non-forest fire, and the most fire on mapped cropland).

- Kubu Raya, West Kalimantan: vegetables and pineapple on peat near Pontianak (burns every year, even in a normal year).

- Sumbawa, Dompu and Bima, West Nusa Tenggara: hillside maize and cattle (the most every-year burning on cropland).

Each area offers its current practice plus three no-burn alternatives, such as mung bean or maize after rice, straw baling or a decomposer, no-burn land preparation with lime or compost, rice with fish or ducks, maize stalks kept as cattle feed, peat restoration, and tree crops on steep slopes. Safety caveats are built in: no draining deep peat, rewetting is a village decision, trees only with land rights, off-season crops only where water allows.

HOW IT WORKS

Python scripts download NASA FIRMS active fires (VIIRS 375 m, 2015-2025), NASA GPM IMERG monthly rain (0.1°, 2001-2024), NASA SMAP soil moisture (9 km, every third day 2015-2025, via Earthdata cloud OPeNDAP), NASA POWER daily weather (2001-2025, one point per area) and SoilGrids soil (250 m). ESA WorldCover separates non-forest fire from forest fire and marks farm land.

ONE GRID FOR DIFFERENT RESOLUTIONS

Before any scoring, every dataset is brought to the same unit: farm land within 8 km of each of 42 districts, by calendar month. GPM cells within 8 km are averaged, SMAP uses the 9 km cell at the district, and SoilGrids takes the median of farm pixels (0-30 cm). Each month then gets an average-year and a dry-year value (the driest fifth of years). The features feed the comparison with stated reasons: each district's own GPM rain sets its wet window; very dry SMAP topsoil at sowing in a dry year lowers an option's safety score (SMAP readings pass its own quality flags at only 6 of 42 districts, so elsewhere the check is skipped rather than guessed); acid soil (for beans) and heavy clay (for upland crops after rice) add warnings. The scripts compute each area's peak burning months, in how many of 11 years fire was seen near each district, dry months, the driest fifth of years, and heavy-rain days. Transparent rules score each option on six goals; for example, they check whether a new crop fits the wet window after harvest in a normal and a dry year (mung bean after rice in Chum Saeng needs about 60 days, gets about 16 days of rain after harvest, and about 136 days with irrigation). Every score carries a reason, shown as a plain sentence in the farmer's language. The site is static, with no server or API key at runtime, and the farmer page needs no map service and loads about 150 KB over the network in total, including two small satellite images.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It puts 11 years of satellite fire records and 25 years of climate data behind each farmer's own decision, is honest about risk and uncertainty, speaks the farmer's language, and targets the burning season.

LIMITATIONS (stated in the app and README)

This is a prototype. Several options manage crop waste rather than change the rotation. The satellite features are coarse (GPM 0.1°, SMAP 9 km) and SoilGrids is a model, not a soil test; the thresholds that turn them into warnings are rules of thumb. The evidence levels come from a quick check of published sources, not a field survey. Crop facts are AI-drafted placeholders; district coordinates are approximate; translations are drafts. On peat, non-forest fire is mostly burnt scrub, so it marks land clearing as much as crop residue.

Next steps: review by agriculture offices and native speakers, field-level checks of the soil and moisture thresholds, assessment of the impact of El Nino/La Nina years, and separating sugarcane from rice burning.

TOOLS

Python (requests, pandas, numpy, rasterio, PyYAML, Pillow), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Leaflet (landing and data pages only), Vercel and GitHub.
